title: Mohanlal vs Shivraj Relhan on 17 November, 2018
full_text: Mohanlal vs Shivraj Relhan on 17 November, 2018 IN THE COURT OF MS. DR. NEERA BHARIHOKE ADDL. SESSIONS JUDGE­06:SOUTH EAST SAKET COURT: NEW DELHI IN RE: Criminal Appeal No.44/2018 Mohanlal S/o Late Sh. Pati Ram R/o RZ­161/1, Gali No.1, Tughlakabad Extension, New Delhi ­110019 ..........Appellant Versus Shivraj Relhan S/o Late Sh. Nihal Chand R/o 1765, Gali No.6, Govindpuri Extension, Kalkaji, New Delhi­110019 ........Respondent ________________________________________________________ Date of Institution : 12.01.2018 Date of arguments : 03.11.2018 Date of judgment : 17.11.2018 J U D G M E N T 1. The present appeal has been filed by the appellant against the impugned Judgment dated 20.11.2017 and order on sentence dated CA No.44/18 1 of 14 19.12.2017 in CC No. 615539/16 titled "Shivraj Ralhan Vs. Mohan Lal", whereby the appellant has been convicted for the offence punishable under section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter to be referred as " N.I. Act ") and vide order dated 19.12.2017, appellant has been sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of 12 months one year and also directed to pay compensation of Rs.3,30,000/­ and in default of payment of compensation, he was directed to be sentenced to further undergo simple imprisonment for one month. 2. This judgment is confined to the objection that the complaint case filed by the respondent under section 138 of NI Act before the learned trial court was not maintainable as the same was filed before expiry of 15 days of refusal of the notice of demand and thus no offence was committed by the appellant as per mandate of section 138 of NI Act as there was no complaint in the eyes of law on the date of filing. 3. Without adverting to the merits of the appeal/complaint case filed before learned trial court, the relevant fact to decide the said objection is that the respondent/complainant allegedly issued notice of demand dated 11.07.2013 to the appellant/accused which was alleged to have been posted on 11.07.2013 itself. The postal receipts, (Ex. CW­1/D and Ex. CW­1/E before the learned trial court) reflect that some articles were sent/posted on 11.07.2013 at 15.12 CA No.44/18 2 of 14 p.m. and 15.13 p.m. respectively. Objection raised by the appellant: 4. No tracking reports of the said articles were filed on record. Ex. CW­1/F filed before the learned trial court reflects the registered article having been received back undelivered and the back side of the envelope contains an endorsement of refusal dated 13.07.2013. In the absence of the tracking report as well as presuming the refusal endorsement dated 13.07.2013 on the back side of an envelope to be correct, the alleged receipt of notice dated 11.07.2013 cannot be presumed to have been delivered before 13.07.2013. Thus the complaint case was not maintainable on 27.07.2013 (on the day on which it was filed) that is before the expiry of 15 days of the service/refusal of the alleged notice of demand. Arguments 5. Learned counsel for appellant has argued that the alleged refusal of the notice of demand dated 11.07.2013 was on 13.07.2013 and thus the respondent could have filed the complaint case against the appellant on or after 28.07.2013 but he filed the same on 27.07.2013 and thus no cognizance of the offence could be taken on the basis of such complaint. 6. On the other hand, learned counsel for respondent has argued CA No.44/18 3 of 14 that there is no merit in the said contention and receipt of summons by learned trial court is also considered as receipt of notice of demand. He also argued that had the appellant any intention to return the money in lieu of which he had issued the cheque in question, he could have made the payment on the day he appeared before the learned trial court after receipt of summons. Learned counsel for appellant has relied on observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the matter titled as Yogendra Pratap Singh vs. Savitri Pandey and another , (2014) 10 SCC 713 where it has been held that any complaint filed before the expiry of 15 days from the date on which the notice has been served on the drawer/accused is no complaint at all in the eye of law and no cognizance of an offence can be taken on the basis of such complaint. 7. Learned counsel for respondent has argued that the law laid down in Yogendra Pratap Singh vs. Savitri Pandey and another (Supra) is not applicable to the case where the notice has not been served upon the accused but has rather been refused by him. He has relied upon the judgment titled Jayakrishnan vs. Unnikrishnan , 2016 (1) Civil Court Cases 008 (Kerala) in support of the submission that in case the demand notice sent to the accused is refused by him or on his behalf, the complainant does not have to wait for a period of 15 days for filing of the complaint case under section 138 of NI Act. CA No.44/18 4 of 14 8. In rebuttal, learned counsel for appellant has argued that Yogendra Pratap Singh vs. Savitri Pandey and another (Supra) is a judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India and no exception is carved out to the law laid down there with regard to the cases where the notice is refused and not received and probably the law laid down in the matter titled Yogendra Pratap Singh vs. Savitri Pandey and another (Supra) was not cited before Hon'ble High Court of Kerala during the course of arguments in the matter titled Jayakrishnan vs. Unnikrishnan, (Supra ). 9. In the matter titled as Yogendra Pratap Singh vs. Savitri Pandey and another , (2014) 10 SCC 713, it has been held that any complaint filed before the expiry of 15 days from the date on which the notice has been served on the drawer/accused is no complaint at all in the eye of law and no cognizance of an offence can be taken on the basis of such complaint. It was also observed that merely because at the time of taking cognizance by the court, the period of 15 days has expired from the date on which the notice had been served on the drawer/accused, the court is not clothed with the jurisdiction to take cognizance of an offence under section 138 on a complaint filed before expiry of 15 days from date of receipt of notice by the drawer of the cheque. Hon'ble Supreme Court of India reaffirmed the view taken by it in Sarav Investment and Financial Consultancy (P) Ltd. vs. Pennar Peterson Securities Ltd., (2000) 2 SCC 745 where it had held that service of notice in terms CA No.44/18 5 of 14 of section 138 proviso (b) of the NI Act was a part of cause of action for lodging the complaint and communication to the accused about the fact of dishonouring of the cheque and calling upon him to pay the amount within 15 days was imperative and corrected, commenced itself to us. It was also observed that no complaint can be maintained against the drawer of the cheque before the expiry of 15 days from the date of receipt of notice because the draw/accused cannot be said to have committed any offence until then. 10. By relying on the law laid down in Jayakrishnan Vs. Unnikrishnan , (supra), learned counsel for respondent had argued that the law laid down in the matter titled as Yogendra Pratap Singh Vs. Savitri Pandey and Another , (supra) would not apply in case of refusal of notice by the accused and thus the respondent/complainant was not required to wait for 15 days to get over from the date of refusal of notice to file the complaint case against the appellant. He has also argued that no such objection was raised by the appellant before learned trial court nor was any such question or suggestion put to the respondent/complainant during his cross­examination before learned trial court. 11. In rebuttal learned counsel for appellant has argued that the objection taken by the appellant is an issue of law and non­raising of the same before learned trial court does not put an embargo upon the appellant in raising it before this court and the same can be CA No.44/18 6 of 14 raised at any point of time/stage. Findings : 12. In the matter of Praveen vs Ismayil , 2005 Cri. LJ 1644, Hon'ble High Court of Kerala observed that: "4. Clause (c) of the proviso to section 138 is very categoric that 15 days for payment of the amount commences from the date of receipt of the notice. If in the case of refusal, it should be 15 days from the date of refusal to accept the notice. The aforesaid fifteen days have therefore to be reckoned in this case from 3.8.96, when the drawer refused to accept notice." 13. In the said case statutory notice was tendered for delivery on the accused and he refused it on 3.8.96. Notice was received back by the complainant on 9.8.96. Hon'ble High Court of Kerala has observed that thus the 15 days have to be reckoned in terms of clause (c) of the proviso to section 138 from the date of receipt of notice by the drawer. In this case, the drawer did have the knowledge about the notice of demand on 3.8.96 when he refused to accept it. So, the payee had to wait until 18.8.96. 14. In the matter of Kunju Viswanandhan vs. Ramakrishnan Surendran, 1998 Cri.LJ 3553, the registered notice sent by the CA No.44/18 7 of 14 appellant intimating about the dishonour of the cheque and calling upon the respondent to pay the amount was refused by the respondent. Though the lower Court found that the respondent issued Ext. P1 cheque to the appellant for the discharge of the debt due from him and the cheque was dishonoured for insufficiency of funds and the registered notice issued by the appellant was refused to be accepted by the respondent, the Court held that the respondent is not guilty of the offence punishable under section 138 of the NI Act since the appellant failed to prove that the complaint was filed before the lower Court after the expiry of 15 days from the receipt of notice as contemplated in Clause (b) of the proviso to section 138 of the NI Act and therefore the complaint was held to have been filed before the cause of action had arisen under Clause (c) of the proviso to section 138 of the NI Act. Undelivered registered notice sent on behalf of the appellant to the respondent bore the endorsement 'refused' by the respondent on 26­5­1990 made by the postal authorities. It was also held that the fact that the registered notice sent on behalf of the appellant to the respondent is refused to accept by the respondent is not disputed. Therefore, the presumptions under section 27 of the General Clauses Act as well as section 114 of the Evidence Act are available in favour of the appellant in this case. Thus raising the presumption of due and proper service. It was observed that consequently it also raises the presumption that the addressee can be imputed with the knowledge of the contents of the registered notice. CA No.44/18 8 of 14 15. It was held that AIR 1981 SC 1284 (1981 All LJ 504) Har Charan Singh v. Shiv Rani lays down the above principles of law. The Hon'ble Kerala High Court observed that the further question to be considered is what is the date of receipt of notice and knowledge of the contents of the notice that can be presumed against the respondent and held that in cases of refusal to accept the notice by the addressee, knowledge of the notice that can be imputed on the addressee is from the date of refusal. It was held that unless and until the 15 days after the receipt of notice by the drawer has elapsed, the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, has no cause of action to file complaint under section 138 of the NI Act. Therefore, expiry of the period of 15 days after the receipt of the notice by the drawer is the pre­requisite or pre­ condition for filing a complaint for the offence punishable under section 138 of the NI Act. 16. Similarly in the matter of N. Venkata Sivaram Prasad vs. Rajeswari Constructions , 1996, Cri.LJ 3409, notice was returned to the appellant by the postal authorities stating that the respondent refused to accept the notice on 27­5­1991. The appellant filed criminal complaint before the II Additional Munsif Magistrate, Chirala on 3­6­1991. Summons were issued on 27­8­1993, the accused was acquitted. The learned Magistrate held that the cause of action for filing the complaint under section 142 of NI Act arose only on 12­6­ 1991 and since the complaint was filed during the pre­offence CA No.44/18 9 of 14 period, the accused cannot be found guilty of the offence under Section 138 of NI Act. The appeal against the said order was dismissed by observing that a reading of section 142 would clearly denote that the cognizance of any offence punishable under section 138 can be taken by the Magistrate provided that on the date of the complaint the offence punishable under section 138 has been made out. It was observed as: "Under section 138 , until and unless the criteria laid down therein are complied with, it would not constitute an offence. Proviso (c) clearly stipulates that the Section does not apply unless the drawer of the cheques fails to make the payment to the payee within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice. Thus, the payee has been given liberty to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of the notice even though the cheque was returned by the Bank unpaid. Hence, the reading of Proviso (c) to section 138 clearly denotes that it would not be an offence if the drawer pays the amount within a period of 15 days as a specified therein. In such circumstances, there could not have been any complaint alleging the violation of section 138 . The pre­offence period granted to the payee should be construed strictly, otherwise the very purpose CA No.44/18 10 of 14 of section 138(c) of the Negotiable Instruments Act would be frustrated. The complainant should be able to point out to the offence under section 138 when the complaint was filed. When the complaint is filed even before the offence is completed, it cannot be said that the offence is made out and, therefore, such complaint is invalid in the eye of law. As already noticed, under section 142 of the Act, no Court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under section 138 , except upon a complaint in writing made by the payee. Therefore, the necessary ingredient enabling the Magistrate to take cognizance of the offence is that there should be a complaint in writing by the payee and the said complaint should disclose an offence under section 138 . In the complaint made by the respondent before the Magistrate, no offence could have been disclosed as the time prescribed under section 138 . Proviso (c) was not exhausted by the time the complaint was presented to the Magistrate. Even by the date of service of summons, there was no further complaint in writing to the effect that even after the expiry of 15 days period as mentioned in proviso (c), the drawer CA No.44/18 11 of 14 failed to pay the amount." 17. The Hon'ble High Court went on to observe that: "If the Magistrate had applied his mind to the question whether the offence under section 138 is made out as per the allegation in the complaint and rejected the complaint at the threshold itself, the delay and unnecessary controversy would have been avoided. The complainant would have known where he stands and he would have preferred a fresh complaint on the expiry of 15 days. Inasmuch as the condition precedent for taking cognizance is the prima facie disclosure of offence based on the allegations in the complaint itself and as the offence was not made out on the date of taking the complaint on file and examining the complainant, the Magistrate instead of taking cognizance of the offence and proceeding further, should have straightway returned the complaint. The Magistrate should not have acted upon the premature complaint which is not a complaint at all in the eye of law." 18. Similar was the decision of Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in the matter titled as Ashok Hegde vs. Jathin V. Attawan , 1997 CA No.44/18 12 of 14 CriLJ 3691 wherein the entire proceedings were quashed as the complaint was filed before the expiry of 15 days from the date of refusal of the notice by holding the complaint to be premature. 19. In the matter of Niranjan Sahoo vs. M/s Utkal Sanitary, 1992 (2) JCC (HC) 42, Hon'ble High Court of Orissa also quashed the order of cognizance as well as the complaint by observing that complainant filed complaint on 13th day of refusal of notice and thus complainant did not give 15 days clear notice to the drawer to comply the notice which means that on the date of filing complaint the complainant had no cause of action. 20. In view of the law aid down in these judgments, I concur with the objection taken by the appellant that since the complaint case was filed by the respondent before learned trial court before the expiry of 15 days from the date of refusal of the notice by the appellant, learned trial court instead of taking cognizance of the offence and proceeding further, should have straightway returned the complaint and should not have acted upon the premature complaint which is not a complaint at all in the eye of law. 21. In the notice framed under section 251 of Cr.P.C. by the learned trial court, it has been wrongly mentioned that "Despite receipt of legal notice dated 11.07.2013, you did not pay the cheque amount to the complainant within stipulated period of 15 days of receipt of CA No.44/18 13 of 14 notice and thereby you have committed an offence punishable under section 138 NI Act." as the complaint case was filed before expiry of 15 days of deemed receipt/refusal of the notice of demand and thus no offence was committed by the appellant as per mandate of section 138 of NI Act as there was no complaint in the eyes of law. 22. In view of these observations, the appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment 20.11.2017 and order on sentence dated 19.12.2017 are set aside. The appellant is held to be not guilty of having committed an offence punishable under section 138 of NI Act and is thus acquitted. 23. A true copy of the judgment alongwith TCR be sent to learned Trial Court for intimation. 24. Appeal file be consigned to record room. Announced in the open (DR.
